title: What Is a Rainforest?
keyIdea: A rainforest is a thick, tall forest in hot, wet places near the Equator where it rains almost every day, so plants grow tall and dense.
familyTip: Point to the Equator on a globe. Say: hot belt, rain most days, tall thick trees. Contrast with a desert photo: both can be hot, but desert is dry.

visual.caption: Rainforest facts — fair idea or myth? Drag each clue, or tap it and then tap a box.

items: rain and warmth grow tall thick trees

lab.caption: Flagship lab: build hot+wet, add rainy days, grow tall trees, point to Equator, reject hot=desert myth, then challenge.

kid: A rainforest is hot and wet.
It rains most days. Trees grow tall and thick.
Rainforests sit near the Equator — the middle line on Earth.
Hot does not mean desert. Deserts are hot and dry. Rainforests are hot and wet.
adult: Early primary geography/science: a rainforest is a thick tall forest that is hot and wet near the Equator. Words: rainforest, Equator, hot, wet, desert, tall, thick. Evidence: describe hot+wet, rain often, Equator belt.
Common mistakes: thinking every hot place is a desert; saying rainforests are cold; thinking it hardly ever rains; placing rainforests at the poles.
In the lab your child turns on hot and wet, adds rainy days, grows tall trees, points to the Equator, and rejects the hot-means-desert myth.

practice.hint: A rainforest needs heat and lots of water together.
practice.explain: Rainforests are hot and wet — unlike hot dry deserts or cold dry places.

practice.hint: Picture rain on most days of the week, not a rare shower.
practice.explain: Rain almost every day is why rainforest plants grow so tall and thick.

practice.prompt: It rained on {a} days. It rained on {b} more days the next week. How many rainy days is that?
practice.hint: Add this week’s rainy days to the extra rainy days next week.
practice.explain: {a} rainy days and {b} more make {=a+b} — rainforests stay wet week after week.

practice.prompt: A poster shows {n} tall rainforest trees. {k} are cut in a drawing. How many tall trees are still standing in the picture?
practice.hint: Count all the tall trees, then take away the ones marked cut.
practice.explain: {n} tall trees minus {k} cut ones leaves {=n-k} still standing in the thick forest.

items: hot and wet near the Equator
practice.hint: Start with place and climate, then rain, then what grows.
practice.explain: Hot wet Equator → rain most days → tall thick trees.

pool.hint: Think of the hot middle belt around Earth, not the poles.
pool.explain: Rainforests grow near the Equator, not at the North Pole or icy Antarctica.

pool.prompt: Is every hot place a desert?
choices: no — a rainforest is hot and wet
pool.hint: Desert is dry; rainforest keeps the rain.
pool.explain: Hot alone is not desert — a rainforest is hot and wet.

pool.prompt: Why do rainforest trees grow so tall?
pool.hint: Plants need both water and warmth to grow huge.
pool.explain: Lots of rain plus warmth grow the tall thick rainforest trees.

choices: a thick tall forest that is hot and wet near the Equator
pool.hint: Bundle hot, wet, Equator and tall thick trees together.
pool.explain: A rainforest is a thick tall forest that is hot and wet near the Equator.

pool.prompt: In one week it rained on {a} days in the rainforest and {b} days in the desert. How many more rainy days did the rainforest have?
pool.hint: Subtract the desert’s rainy days from the rainforest’s.
pool.explain: {a} − {b} = {=a-b} more rainy days in the rainforest than the desert.

pool.prompt: A class names {a} rainforest animals and {b} desert animals. How many animals did they name?
pool.hint: Add the rainforest animal names to the desert animal names on the list.
pool.explain: {a} rainforest animals and {b} desert animals make {=a+b} named altogether.

pool.prompt: Saying rainforests hardly ever get rain is…
choices: a mistake — it rains almost every day
pool.hint: The word rain is part of rainforest — think how often it falls.
pool.explain: Saying it hardly rains is a mistake — rain almost every day feeds the forest.

pool.prompt: Why learn what a rainforest is?
choices: to know hot wet Equator forests with tall trees
to mix them up with deserts
to say they never get rain
pool.hint: Keep the four ideas: hot, wet, Equator, tall trees.
pool.explain: Learning the definition stops mixing rainforests up with dry deserts.
